- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

input.approach_name: Clojure/immer-style persistent bit-partitioned vector trie (branching factor 32) with a shared tail leaf, Rc-based path copying, radix indexing, and a leaf-caching forward iterator — validated against the reference binary via a working prototype
input.data_structure:
CONSTANTS: `const BITS: u32 = 5; const B: usize = 32; const MASK: usize = 31;`

NODE — a two-variant enum, one heap allocation per node, shared via `Rc`:
```rust
enum Node<T> {
    Inner(Vec<Rc<Node<T>>>),  // 1..=32 children, all at the same level
    Leaf(Vec<T>),             // 1..=32 elements (0 only for the empty vector's tail)
}
```
Accessors `fn inner(&self) -> &Vec<Rc<Node<T>>>` and `fn leaf(&self) -> &Vec<T>` panic on the wrong variant; the level/shift bookkeeping guarantees they are never mis-called (the prototype asserted this across 105 cases and never tripped).
Rationale for `Vec` over `[Option<T>; 32]`: no `T: Default`/`Copy` bound, no `Option` tag per slot, and `len()` doubles as the "how many children are populated" counter, which the push path needs. Optional later optimization: `Box<[T]>` / `Box<[Rc<Node<T>>]>` to drop the unused capacity word (see pitfalls).

VECTOR — 4 words + 2 Rc pointers:
```rust
pub struct Vector<T> {
    root:  Rc<Node<T>>,  // ALWAYS Node::Inner. Holds elements [0, tail_offset)
    tail:  Rc<Node<T>>,  // ALWAYS Node::Leaf. Holds elements [tail_offset, size)
    size:  usize,        // total element count
    shift: u32,          // bit-shift for the ROOT level; 5, 10, 15, ...
}
```
`Clone` is derived-equivalent: bump both Rc refcounts, copy `size`/`shift`. O(1).

LEVEL/SHIFT CONVENTION (pin this down; it is the #1 source of off-by-one bugs):
`shift` is the shift applied at the root. A node at level `L` selects its child with `(i >> L) & MASK`; its children are at level `L - 5`; leaves are at level 0. So the root is at level `shift`, and tree depth (in Inner levels) is `shift / 5`.

| shift | root contains        | tree-part capacity      | depth grows at size |
|-------|----------------------|-------------------------|---------------------|
| 5     | Inner of Leaves      | 32^2 = 1 024            | 1 056               |
| 10    | Inner of Inner/Leaf  | 32^3 = 32 768           | 32 800              |
| 15    | ...                  | 32^4 = 1 048 576        | 1 048 608           |
| 20    | ...                  | 32^5 = 33 554 432       | 33 554 464          |

Tree-part capacity at a given shift is exactly `1 << (shift + BITS)`.

KEY DERIVED QUANTITY: `fn tail_offset(&self) -> usize { self.size - self.tail.leaf().len() }` — the number of elements living in the trie. Because only *full* 32-element leaves are ever pushed into the trie, `tail_offset` is always a multiple of 32.

EMPTY VECTOR: `root = Rc::new(Node::Inner(vec![]))`, `tail = Rc::new(Node::Leaf(vec![]))`, `size = 0`, `shift = 5`. This is the only state where a Leaf may be empty; the empty root is never descended into because `tail_offset == 0` routes every index to the tail.

PUBLIC API (mirrors the C++ surface exactly): `new()`, `size() -> usize`, `get(usize) -> &T`, `impl Index<usize>`, `push_back(&self, T) -> Vector<T>` (takes `&self`, returns a new vector — the receiver is untouched), `iter()`, `impl IntoIterator for &Vector<T>`, `impl Default`, `impl Clone`.
key_invariants: `root` is always `Node::Inner`; `tail` is always `Node::Leaf`. Never violated, so the variant accessors never panic.
`shift >= BITS` (minimum 5) and `shift % BITS == 0`. `shift` is the level of the root; children of a node at level L are at level L-5; leaves are at level 0.
`tail_offset == size - tail.len()` and `tail_offset % 32 == 0` — only complete 32-element leaves are ever moved into the trie.
`1 <= tail.len() <= 32` whenever `size > 0`. `tail.len() == 0` iff `size == 0`. The tail is never empty for a non-empty vector, so `push_back` never has to synthesize a tail from the tree.
`tail_offset <= 1 << (shift + BITS)` — the trie at the current shift can hold the whole tree part. Equality means the root is exactly full and the next leaf push must grow depth.

The trie is a PERFECT tree except along its right edge: every Leaf reachable from the root holds exactly 32 elements, and every Inner node except those on the rightmost path holds exactly 32 children. This is what makes radix indexing valid with no per-node size table (unlike a relaxed RRB-tree).

The leaf slot targeted by a tail flush is always fresh: at level 5, `(tail_offset >> 5) & MASK == children.len()`, so the insert is always a `push` onto the end, never an overwrite. (Asserted in the prototype; never tripped.)

Nodes are immutable once wrapped in `Rc`. Every mutation allocates new nodes along one root-to-leaf path (path copying) and shares all off-path subtrees by refcount bump. No `Rc::get_mut`/`make_mut` anywhere.
Element `i` lives in the tail iff `i >= tail_offset`, otherwise in the trie. `get` must test this FIRST.
Structural sharing is real and load-bearing: verified empirically that 200,000 coexisting versions of a 200k-element vector consume 49 MB rather than the 78 GB deep copying would require.
module_layout: `Cargo.toml` — `[package] name/version`, `edition = "2021"`, `rust-version = "1.75"`, and an EMPTY `[dependencies]` section (zero external crates). Add `[profile.release] overflow-checks = false` only as belt-and-braces; correctness must not depend on it because all arithmetic uses explicit `wrapping_*`.

`src/main.rs` — the program: `stoi`-compatible arg parsing (default `n = 11` when `argc <= 1`), the two push/sum loops with explicit wrapping arithmetic, and `println!` + flush per output line. Declares `mod vector; mod stoi;`.

`src/vector/mod.rs` — `pub struct Vector<T>` and its inherent impls: `new`, `size`, `tail_offset`, `leaf_for`, `get`, `iter`; plus `impl Index<usize>`, `impl Clone`, `impl Default`, `impl IntoIterator for &Vector<T>`, and (optional, nice for tests) `impl Debug`/`FromIterator`. Declares `mod node; mod iter;` and re-exports `pub use iter::Iter;`.

`src/vector/node.rs` — `pub(crate) enum Node<T>`, the `BITS`/`B`/`MASK` constants, the `inner()`/`leaf()` accessors, and the free functions `new_path` and `push_leaf`. All the bit-twiddling lives here and nowhere else.

`src/stoi.rs` — `pub fn stoi(s: &str) -> Result<i32, StoiError>` replicating `std::stoi`, and a helper that mimics an uncaught C++ exception (exact stderr text + abort). Kept separate so it can be unit-tested against the reference binary's observed behavior.

`src/vector/tests.rs` (or `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside `mod.rs`) — unit tests for: the depth-growth boundaries (sizes 1055/1056/1057, 32799/32800/32801, 1048607/1048608/1048609); `get(i) == i+1` for all i at each of those sizes; iterator order and length equal to indexed order; and the persistence property that N intermediate versions held simultaneously each retain exactly their own prefix.

`tests/differential.rs` (optional integration test) — shells out to `/workspace/dataset/test11_executable` and compares stdout for a list of n values plus random n, exactly as I did while validating the prototype.
pitfalls: SIGNED OVERFLOW IS LOAD-BEARING AND WILL PANIC IN DEBUG BUILDS. The reference relies on `int` wraparound; I confirmed it: n=1048576 prints `524288` (true sum 549 756 338 176 ≡ 524 288 mod 2^32), n=65536 prints `-2147450880`, n=46341 prints `1073767311` then `-2147432674` (first sum positive, second wrapped negative), n=92681 prints `-37075` then `-74150`. Plain `sum += x` panics with 'attempt to add with overflow' under `cargo build`/`cargo test`. Use `wrapping_add`/`wrapping_mul` explicitly so debug and release agree; do NOT rely on release-mode wrapping or on an `overflow-checks = false` profile flag.

`v[i] * 2` needs `wrapping_mul(2)` as well, not just the accumulator. It only overflows for elements above 2^30 (requiring n > 1.07e9, impractical to run) but silent-panic-vs-wrap divergence there is still a latent bug.

SHIFT/LEVEL OFF-BY-ONE is the classic failure. Fix the convention once: `shift` is the ROOT's level; a node at level L indexes with `(i >> L) & MASK`; children are at `L - 5`; leaves are at level 0; `new_path(level, leaf)` returns a subtree whose root is AT `level`, so callers pass `level - BITS`. Getting this wrong yields a tree that works up to 1024 elements and breaks at 1056.

The root-overflow test must be driven by `tail_offset` (elements in the trie), not `size`. Correct form: `(tail_offset >> BITS) + 1 > (1usize << shift)`. Using `size` mis-fires by one leaf and corrupts the tree at depth transitions.

Test the exact depth-growth sizes, not just powers of 32. Depth grows when `tail_offset` hits `32^k`, i.e. at SIZE `32^k + 32`: 1056, 32800, 1048608, 33554464. Testing only 1024/32768 misses the bug entirely. My prototype matched the reference at 1055/1056/1057, 32799/32800/32801 and 1048607/1048608/1048609.

`let toff = self.size - B;` in the tail-flush branch underflows if reached with a non-full tail. It is only correct under the `tail.len() == B` guard — keep the branch structure as written and never reorder the `tl < B` test.

Do NOT deep-clone subtrees in the path copy. `node.inner().clone()` on a `Vec<Rc<Node<T>>>` clones 32 Rc HANDLES (refcount bumps), which is the whole point. If `Node` ever derives `Clone` structurally over `T`, an accidental `(*node).clone()` silently turns O(log n) into O(n) and destroys sharing. Prefer not deriving `Clone` on `Node` at all.

Adopt the full tail into the trie by `self.tail.clone()` (Rc bump), NOT by cloning its `Vec<T>` into a new `Node::Leaf`. Copying costs 32 elements per flush for zero benefit, and storing the tail as `Rc<Node<T>>` (rather than `Rc<Vec<T>>`) is what makes the bump possible — this is also what immer does.

Implement `IntoIterator` for `&Vector<T>`, not for `Vector<T>`. The program iterates `v` and then indexes it again afterward; a consuming iterator will not compile against that usage and would misrepresent the immutable contract.

Never use `Rc::make_mut`/`Rc::get_mut` to mutate a node in place. `push_back` takes `&self`, so the receiver always holds a reference and the refcount is >= 1 — `make_mut` would copy anyway, but reaching for it invites a real aliasing bug the moment someone adds a `&mut self` fast path.

Do not build the iterator as `(0..size).map(|i| v.get(i))`. It is correct but re-descends per element; measurably ~4x slower at 20M elements. Cache the leaf slice and refill only on the 1-in-32 boundary crossing.

`std::stoi` semantics are NOT `str::parse::<i32>()`. Verified against the binary: leading ASCII whitespace is skipped (`" 7"`→7, `"\t5"`→5, `"\n6"`→6), an optional `+`/`-` sign is accepted (`"+9"`→9, `"-5"`→-5), parsing stops at the first non-digit WITHOUT error (`"12abc"`→12, `"0x10"`→0), no digits at all throws `invalid_argument` (`"abc"`, `""`), and out-of-int-range throws `out_of_range`. `str::parse` rejects `"12abc"` and `" 7"`, so hand-roll it. Accumulate in `i64` and range-check against `i32::MIN..=i32::MAX` (and treat digit runs long enough to overflow `i64` as out_of_range).

Negative or zero n must produce `0\n0\n`, not a panic: the push loop simply does not execute and `0..v.size()` is empty. Confirmed `-1` and `-5` both print `0` `0` with exit 0. Extra trailing argv entries are ignored.

For an uncaught-exception input, the reference writes to STDERR and aborts with shell-reported exit 134 (SIGABRT), printing exactly (note the two-space indents, byte-verified with `od -c`): `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'\n  what():  stoi\n`. Emit that verbatim to stderr, write nothing to stdout, and exit 134 (`std::process::exit(134)`; or `std::process::abort()` if the harness inspects the real signal).

`std::endl` flushes. Rust's stdout is line-buffered to a TTY but BLOCK-buffered to a pipe. `println!` twice then a normal exit still flushes, but if you ever swap in a `BufWriter` or call `process::exit` early, output can be lost — flush explicitly after each line to match `endl`.

Recursion depth in `push_leaf`, `new_path`, and the implicit `Drop` of `Rc<Node<T>>` is bounded by tree depth (<= 13 even for usize::MAX elements), so there is NO stack-overflow risk here — unlike a persistent linked list. Do not over-engineer an iterative drop.

Per-node `Vec` costs three words (ptr/len/cap) plus a separate allocation; that is the entire ~2.5x gap I measured versus the C++ reference at 20M elements. If that matters, switch node payloads to `Box<[T]>`/`Box<[Rc<Node<T>>]>` (drops the cap word) — but only after the differential tests pass, since it complicates the `push` path.
rust_1_75_concerns: Everything in this design is stable well before 1.75 — `Rc`, enums, slices, `wrapping_*`, `ExactSizeIterator`, `impl Index`. I compiled and ran the full prototype under the exact toolchain present here (`rustc 1.75.0 (82e1608df 2023-12-21)`) with no feature gates and no warnings.
Do NOT reach for `impl Trait` in associated type position / RPITIT for the iterator — not stable in 1.75. Use the explicit named `Iter<'a, T>` struct with `type IntoIter = Iter<'a, T>` as specified.
Avoid `let ... else` chained with complex patterns and any `async fn` in traits; neither is needed. `let else` itself IS stable in 1.75 (since 1.65) if you want it for the stoi parser.
